entry.title: [Soroushdabbagh_Official] The murmurings of 14. Sohrab in the notebook "The Traveler" and "The Green…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @Soroushdabbagh_Official

The murmurings of 14. Sohrab in the notebook "The Traveler" and "The Green Volume" was murmuring to himself: "The lover is always alone/ and the lover's hand is in the trembling hand of seconds/...He and the seconds sleep on light/ and he and the seconds give the best book in the world/ to the water/ and they know well/ that no fish ever/ untied the thousand and one knots of the river/ and at midnights with the old boat of illumination/ they set out on the waters of guidance/ and drive on until the manifestation of wonder." And: "Someone came and took my books/ drew a ceiling of the harmony of flowers over my head/ made my evening vast with repeated windows/ placed my table under the spirituality of rain." The contemplative Shirazi mystic also whispered to himself: "Seize the moment and drink in the rose garden, for the rose will not be there another week. Tear up the pages if you are my fellow student, for the knowledge of love is not in the notebook." And: "Speak of the minstrel and wine and seek less the secret of time, for no one has unraveled and no one will unravel this riddle through philosophy." And: "What is this tall ceiling, simple yet of many patterns? Of this riddle, no sage in the world is aware." What a strange creature the human being is! A two-legged migratory bird who passes night and day in this existence, estranged, in toil and turmoil. On one hand, he knows that acquiring knowledge and understanding is, in Aristotle's words, among the "virtues" that constitute the essence of your and my humanity; a knowledge found in books and notebooks that draws the wise in its wake. On the other hand, he sees wayfarers like Hafez and Sepehri, who were learned and erudite, at a stage of their existential journey laying down their shields, acknowledging the enigmatic and mysterious nature of existence, relinquishing the untying of knots, washing away the pages of lessons and exercises and notebooks and books and entrusting them to flowing water, placing "the burden of knowledge from the shoulders of the swallow onto the ground"; and they have tasted and savored a "transparent fear," a "wise silence," and a strange wonder and bewilderment that consumes the palate.

Quoted from the book: "Velvety Murmurings," Volume Two.
Author: Soroush Dabbagh

entry.title: [jalaeipour] The next war doesn't necessarily begin with the firing of the first missile.…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @jalaeipour

The next war doesn't necessarily begin with the firing of the first missile. Before that, a battle is already underway — over truth, over assigning blame, over legitimizing military action. Who broke the agreement? Who started the conflict? Who will bear responsibility for the consequences of the next war? The answers to these questions may be constructed and locked in on the media battlefield before the military conflict even begins.

Take the narrative that has taken shape in recent days around attacks on oil tankers and commercial ships: that Iran deliberately violated the Islamabad Understanding and is therefore responsible for the collapse of the agreement and the possible escalation of war. That the attacks occurred is one thing; turning that into a definitive narrative of Iran's unilateral responsibility — without examining the obligations of the parties, the US naval blockade, and the sequence of military actions — is another. Sometimes, to build a misleading narrative, there's no need to fabricate reality at all; it's enough to select part of the truth and omit the rest.

We have seen this before, too, in attempts to discredit real images of the bombing of Tehran. Some media accounts claimed the images of destruction were staged and that the women seen in the photos were actresses who kept reappearing. An independent review of the images from Sabounchi Street in Tehran refuted that claim. Here, the issue wasn't merely the publication of a false news item; it was an attempt to make the audience doubt reality itself, even when confronted with documented images of destruction and war victims.

In the possible next stage of the war, we must be more vigilant than ever against three phenomena: Misinformation — false information spread unknowingly; Disinformation — fake and distorted information deliberately produced to deceive; and Malinformation — real information used to cause harm, for example by revealing the identity or location of individuals at risk. These three can be deployed simultaneously to sow panic, destroy public trust, deny the realities of war, and prepare public opinion to accept a new conflict.

In such conditions, the war propaganda headquarters, if it exists, must monitor the information space moment by moment and respond with speed, accuracy, and verifiable evidence. Of course, countering information warfare doesn't mean constructing counter-narratives or denying unpleasant realities. The main capital in this battle is public trust, and that capital is preserved only through honesty and transparency.

The war of narratives may, before the military war, produce one crucial outcome: whom the public considers the initiator of the war, whom it recognizes as the victim, and whom it holds responsible for the destruction that follows.

📢 Twelve water and electricity projects inaugurated in East Azerbaijan with a budget of 124,500 billion tomans

◀️ In the presence of Mohammad Jafar Qaempanah, Executive Deputy to the President, during a visit to East Azerbaijan province today, 23 Mehr, 12 projects — including 2 water and wastewater projects and 10 electricity infrastructure projects — with a total announced budget of 124,500 billion tomans were inaugurated.

◀️ Among the inaugurated projects are a water supply project serving 150 villages in the province with a budget of 665 billion tomans, and the Azarshahr wastewater treatment plant with its transmission and collection network, Module One, with a budget of 1,740 billion tomans, both implemented by the East Azerbaijan Water and Wastewater Company.

◀️ The water supply project for 150 villages includes drilling and equipping 25 wells, building 19 reservoirs, laying 165 kilometers of transmission lines and 137 kilometers of water distribution network, rehabilitating 12 kilometers of transmission line, and constructing 6 pumping stations. With this project coming online, a stable water supply will be provided for 150 villages comprising 10,427 households and a population of over 36,745.

◀️ The Azarshahr wastewater treatment plant, using the advanced SBR method with a daily treatment capacity of 8,100 cubic meters, will serve a population of over 84,000.

◀️ Additionally, 10 electricity infrastructure projects under the responsibility of the East Azerbaijan Regional Electricity Company have been inaugurated. These projects include a 230-kilovolt double-circuit cable line to supply the central GIS substation of Tabriz via the energy tunnel, the 230-kilovolt section of the central GIS substation of Tabriz, and eight line and substation projects.

◀️ The total expenditure for the electricity projects is announced at 11,095 billion tomans, and their implementation has created jobs for 400 people. The goals of these projects include increasing the reliability of electricity supply to central Tabriz and its subordinate counties, and meeting the electricity needs of industrial parks.

Varisha Moradi's lawyers announced on Wednesday, 22 Mehr, that Branch 15 of the Tehran Revolutionary Court — which had previously sentenced this political prisoner held in Evin to execution on charges of "membership in a rebel group" — insisted on its previous death sentence despite the Supreme Court's request to examine "deficiencies in the investigation."

Amir Sajjadi and Keyvan Azizi, Varisha Moradi's lawyers, speaking to "Emtedad," confirmed this news and stated that on Wednesday, 22 Mehr, they visited Branch 15 of the Revolutionary Court and received the verdict issued by this branch, and according to the notified verdict, they have 20 days to appeal to the Supreme Court.

According to them, this verdict was issued in a situation where the previous verdict of Branch 15 sentencing Varisha Moradi to death had been overturned by the reviewing branch in the Supreme Court after serious doubts were raised about the investigation; yet the aforementioned branch, without conducting the investigation requested by the Supreme Court, merely changed the title of the charge and once again sentenced Ms. Moradi to execution on the charge of membership in a rebel group.

Amir Sajjadi, stating that "in the lawyers' view, there are no sufficient and solid grounds for attributing such a charge to Varisha Moradi," emphasized: "Ms. Moradi has absolutely not been involved in any operations against the Islamic Republic, and her activities were solely related to her fight against ISIS in northern Syria."

Keyvan Azizi also, emphasizing that Varisha Moradi's lawyers will appeal within the legal deadline, expressed hope that "the Supreme Court, as in the previous instance, will give sufficient attention to the defenses and objections."

Varisha Moradi, who is currently imprisoned in Evin Prison, was arrested on 10 Mordad 1402 on the outskirts of Sanandaj, and on 5 Dey of the same year, upon completion of the interrogation stages, was transferred from the Ministry of Intelligence detention center known as Ward 209 of Evin Prison to the women's ward of this prison.

She was sentenced to execution on 20 Aban 1403 by Branch 15 of the Tehran Revolutionary Court on charges of "baghy" (armed uprising against the government). In an open letter from prison, she revealed that during her detention she was subjected to physical and psychological torture, death threats, and gender-based violence.

@VahidHeadline📡 @VahidOnline

entry.title: [darvishnameh] 💧 Environmental water rights: from allocation on paper to water reaching the…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @darvishnameh

💧 Environmental water rights: from allocation on paper to water reaching the wetland

The report "Regulatory Oversight of Environmental Water Rights Allocation under Table (7) of Article (37) of the Seventh Development Plan Law," prepared by Mehdi Rajabi and Ali Haji-Moradi in Shahrivar 1405, examines the gap between legal commitments and the actual delivery of water needed by ecosystems.

The report's findings for the water year 1403–1404 show that drought is not the only reason water rights are not being fulfilled; weaknesses in the allocation system, withdrawals along the route, lack of coordination among agencies, and the absence of transparent monitoring also play a role.

The report's central message is clear: releasing water from a dam alone does not mean environmental water rights have been secured. The evaluation criterion must be whether water reaches the target ecosystem, in a volume, quality, and timing suited to its needs.

The report emphasizes reforming water allocation under water-scarce conditions, online monitoring and public disclosure of data, controlling withdrawals along the route, and integrated management of river basins.

🌱 Environmental water rights must hold a stable place in water allocation decisions — a share whose provision does not depend on water left over after other uses.

#Environmental_Water_Rights #Water_Governance #Wetlands #Seventh_Plan #Parliament_Research_Center

entry.title:
[bamotamem] Large World Models (LWMs)
This conversation I had with ChatGPT is not an ideal…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @bamotamem

Large World Models (LWMs)

This conversation I had with ChatGPT is not an ideal example and is even somewhat misleading.

But it can show to some extent the difference between a language model and a world model.

The current wave of AI will presumably subside after the current bubble bursts (and of course its amazing achievements and capabilities will still remain with us).

In the next wave, we will encounter large models of the world, or LWMs, or Large World Models, which have a better understanding of what is possible and impossible in the physical world.

Of course, even now the models that Tesla uses in the automotive industry and Palantir uses in war are of the World Model type. But still, whether from the perspective of technology and system architecture or from the perspective of commercial and widespread access, we are very far from "artificial intelligence capable of understanding the physical world."

This gap — contrary to all the hype — is not only a matter of scale.

Failure of the National Suicide Prevention Program

Hamid Peyravi, secretary of the Suicide Prevention Taskforce of Tehran Province, acknowledging the rising suicide rates in Iran, noted: One reason for the increase in statistics since the 1380s could be the systematization of case recording. In other words, before the 80s, cases were not recorded properly, and once accurate and precise recording was put on the agenda, naturally the statistics go up.

He referred to the issuance of the National Suicide Prevention Program in Shahrivar of 1401 and said: The plan was that in the final year of the program — that is, this year — we would achieve a 10 percent reduction in suicide attempts and deaths caused by it, but unfortunately we did not reach the program's goals at all; there has even been an increase, especially in attempts.

The vice president of the Scientific Society for Suicide Prevention in Iran called suicide bereavement one of the worst and most complicated types of grief and said: Individuals blame themselves, feel guilt, engage in self-rumination, or are subjected to society's judgment and are rejected.

He continued: More than 7,000 deaths and more than 150,000 suicide attempts in a single year have affected a large number of Iranian families, but has anyone reached out to these families? How do they cope with this suffering, and do they seek help?

Peyravi said: Each suicide involves and affects 135 people, and therefore the scope of our work goes beyond the numbers that are announced.

If Hitler had been killed... On March 13, 1930, just as the car carrying Hitler entered the intersection, a large truck came speeding into the intersection from the right and slammed into the right side of Hitler's car. The exact side where Hitler was sitting in the front seat, next to his driver. The truck pushed the car to the other side of the intersection and came to a stop just before it could run over the car and crush it along with everyone inside. Hitler asked loudly, "Is everyone still alive?" Everyone survived. Though Hitler and two other occupants were left with bruises and contusions. Three years later, he became Chancellor of Germany, and what followed was the carnage of World War II and the Holocaust — a slaughter that claimed tens of millions of lives. If the truck had crushed the car and Hitler had been killed, would those deaths still have happened?

"We and Gazprom": A Documentary Account of Why Iran's Gas Industry Fell Behind

The second episode of the "5 Khordad" podcast, titled "We and Gazprom," was screened today at the Atana Hotel in Tehran, attended by members of the Energy Commission of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, former and current energy officials, experts, and journalists. The documentary reviews Russia's experience in developing its gas industry to examine the obstacles facing the development of this industry in Iran and the role of Tehran-Moscow gas relations.

Focusing on the history of Russia's oil and gas industry, particularly the formation and expansion of the country's gas distribution network, the documentary seeks to examine the development paths of the gas industry in both Iran and Russia through the lens of historical experiences and strategic decisions.

In this episode, through conversations with veterans and experts of the gas industry, the question is raised: why has Iran, despite holding the world's second-largest natural gas reserves, been unable to develop its gas industry in proportion to its resource capacity and secure a more influential position in regional and global markets?

One of the documentary's central themes is the relationship between the abundance of gas resources, domestic pricing policy, and the development of gas industry infrastructure. Has the supply of cheap gas to consumers contributed to the sustainable development of this industry, or have pricing policies and rising domestic consumption constrained the resources needed for infrastructure investment and export development? The documentary seeks to examine various dimensions of this issue by presenting expert perspectives.

In another section, the documentary turns its attention to Iran-Russia gas relations—two countries that rank among the world's largest holders of natural gas reserves yet have taken different paths in developing gas exports. In this context, the question is raised: has Russia obstructed Iran's gas export development in recent years, and what impact has competition between the two countries had on Iran's export opportunities?

To watch the second episode of the "5 Khordad" podcast titled "We and Gazprom," follow the link below:

Data Colonialism The Data-Devouring of Tech Giants and…
entry.summary:

🎊🎊 Just Published

Data Colonialism
The Data-Devouring of Tech Giants and Ways to Resist It
Analysis by Makhia, Nick Couldry
Translated by Hossein Sheikh-Rezaei
Science and Technology Studies Series / Director: Hossein Sheikh-Rezaei
356 pages / 1,250,000 Toman
View and purchase from the Kargadan website:
www.kargadanpub.com

🔸 Postcolonial studies centered on data and cyberspace help us understand that emerging technologies do not take shape in a social and political vacuum. Data, algorithms, and artificial intelligence, like any other technology, are constructed within power relations. The question is not "What technologies do we have?" but rather "Who designs them, what interests are involved in their deployment, and which groups benefit from their advantages and disadvantages?"

🔸 The authors of this book remind us that colonialism should not be defined merely in its historical form, including the occupation of territory and the creation of colonies. Colonialism has taken different forms throughout history and continues today in a new guise, including control over data extraction infrastructures and technological dependency. In the digital age, human data, social behaviors, and collective information have become resources that are collected from around the world and processed, accumulated, and made the basis for decision-making in a few centers.

🔸 The concept of "data colonialism" introduced by the authors of the book emphasizes precisely this aspect. The issue is not that data is inherently negative or that digital technology should be abandoned; the issue is that in the current global order, ownership and control of data are severely unbalanced and are mainly in the hands of large tech giants, who use it for profit, predicting collective behaviors, and even political influence.

🔸 In addition to theoretical analyses and case studies, the authors also propose solutions for countering data colonialism in the present era.

entry.summary:

Source: @bamotamem

In the Motamem systems thinking discussion about Jared Diamond, one of the members had quoted something from Jared Diamond, and it occurred to me to write a bit there about his latest book, which was published last month. Naturally, there's more room for writing at length on Motamem. But still, I can share a few general points here as well:🖋️ In this book (and in almost all his books from the past thirty years), Diamond is pondering this question: which is greater — the power of "systems and structure" or the power of "people"?I think we Iranians are constantly thinking about this very question. That if so-and-so hadn't been there or hadn't come in such-and-such a year, or if someone else had come instead of someone else, how much would our historical trajectory have changed?🖋️ There are plenty of fascinating points and instructive stories in this book. But methodologically and analytically, I think it's weaker than Diamond's previous works. Still, by a wide margin, Guns, Germs, and Steel remains his best book.🖋️ Diamond believes in the power of influence for both individuals and systems. But he considers the effect of individuals greater in the short term and the effect of systems greater in the long term.🖋️ Diamond is old. One should always view the latest works of thinkers and writers with a forgiving eye. Because their goal is to deliver their remaining notes to us.
---

🔹The main danger, however, is the pulse of negotiation at a moment when the perception of non-victory has not yet taken hold in the enemy.
🔹A signal of dialogue under these conditions is no free lunch, and it can muddy the message of power and hand time back to the opponent's favor.
🔹In a siege, trial and error is a luxury. Iran must compress time, not sell it off through hesitation. Peace comes when the opponent comes to believe that victory is impossible.

entry.title: [VahidOnline] Shahrzad Shahbazi, one of the lawyers for the defendants in the "Aliakhani…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @VahidOnline

Shahrzad Shahbazi, one of the lawyers for the defendants in the "Aliakhani Square of Isfahan" case and the lawyer for Alireza Sepahi, has rejected the narrative put forward by state media, announcing that the charge of killing law enforcement officers was never communicated to any of the defendants in this case, nor did the court address this charge. So far, five of the defendants in this case have been executed, and seven others remain at risk of execution. The lawyer's statements came in response to the publication of an interview in state media in which a woman, introduced as the wife of one of the killed officers, accuses the defendants of killing and burning officers. The interview was published after criticism mounted over the carrying out of executions, particularly the execution of Alireza Sepahi. Shahbazi also questioned the presence of this woman at the site of the executions, asking: when the case did not involve qisas or a personal right, on what basis was she allowed to be present at the site where the sentence was carried out? In a message posted on Instagram on Saturday, 18 Mehr 1405, Shahbazi wrote: "The charge of killing has under no circumstances been communicated to any of the defendants in the Aliakhani Square and Shohada Square case." She emphasized that the allegation of "burning officers in connection with premeditated murder" was neither addressed in court nor included among the charges in the verdict. Shahbazi cited the Revolutionary Court's lack of jurisdiction over this charge as the reason it did not take up the matter of killing. The Aliakhani Square case was opened after four Special Unit officers were killed during the protests of 18 Dey 1404 in Isfahan. State media had previously published videos of the defendants' confessions during interrogations, crime scene reconstructions, and trial sessions in Branch One of the Isfahan Revolutionary Court — confessions that human rights bodies consider forced and invalid. Alireza Sepahi was executed in the early hours of Monday, 13 Mehr. Mai Sato, the United Nations Special Rapporteur on human rights in Iran, in reaction to the execution, had reported serious concerns about the torture of defendants and the lack of a fair trial in this case. According to Sato, the sentence was carried out while Sepahi's lawyer was still working to have the case reviewed. Sepahi had previously also been on the verge of public execution, but was transferred to the hospital after a heart attack. That same night, citizens stayed in Aliakhani Square until dawn to prevent the executions from being carried out.@VahidHeadline📡 @VahidOnline

entry.title: [darvishnameh] Shahvar!✍Yaser Arab For fifteen years, they cut down the trees, slashed the…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @darvishnameh

Shahvar!✍Yaser Arab
For fifteen years, they cut down the trees, slashed the bushes, displaced the animals, destroyed the birds' nests, and carved up the body of Mount Shahvar — this source of water, bread, and life for the people — and most of us just watched, without understanding what was being lost!

Some thought, what does one mountain matter? What harm could it do to take a piece of a mountain?

They didn't understand that Shahvar is not just stone, not just a home for bears, not just a shelter for birds, not just the memory of the forest — but a part of the life cycle on which the life of the plains, agriculture, and the people of Bastam and Shahroud depend, to which they are bound.

Those who saw the stone but not the water, who saw the mine but not the land. Those who failed to understand that the wound being inflicted today on the body of Mount Shahvar can tomorrow turn into the thirst of the earth, the pollution of water, and the endless suffering of the people — they must be held accountable today!

Now Shahvar remains; wounded and silent. A Shahvar that seems to have become a Shahzar for years, weeping bitterly to itself.

But it is no longer time for mourning alone. It is time to stand, time to ask, time to demand answers from those who allowed this wound to deepen every day for fifteen years!

@yaser_arab57

entry.title: [mostafamalekian] 🔴I Have Not Been Happy ✍️ From an interview with Mostafa Malekian.…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @mostafamalekian

🔴I Have Not Been Happy ✍️ From an interview with Mostafa Malekian. Published in Andishe Pouya 102

You have always said that spirituality is a process that brings tranquility, joy, and hope. As you pass seventy, have you yourself attained this tranquility, joy, and hope?

🔹As for tranquility, I am content and I believe I have it. As for hope, I am also content. But joy, no. From childhood onward, I think — perhaps due to my psychological makeup, or perhaps due to my childhood environment — I have fundamentally never been happy. This one thing I truly lack, and I have never truly laughed from the bottom of my heart; never.

Looking back on your life from the vantage point of seventy, what was the hardest period of your life? And what was the most precious price you paid for intellectual honesty?

🔹I think the most precious price I paid was losing friends. I am a person who cherishes friendship, and friendship matters greatly to me. To this day, I myself have never cut ties with anyone. But with every intellectual transformation I underwent, I lost a number of friends for whom I was very dear. It was as though their beliefs mattered more to them, and when I changed my beliefs, they would sever their friendship with me.

🔹The hardest period of my life was when I forsook many outward trappings and privileges in order to bring about, in my own estimation, a transformation in the Qom seminary. At that time I was also devout in every sense; out of compassion and mercy, I wanted the educational, training, and research system of the seminary to change so that the very goals they held would be realized and achieved in the best possible way. For example, I myself began changing the textbooks — that is, I was teaching, but not with the seminary textbooks, rather with books I deemed better. But gradually I saw that I was far too small to accomplish anything against this very old edifice. During those eighteen years in which I wanted to do something in Qom, I was awarded a scholarship twice to be sent abroad, and I went neither time. It always seemed to me that if this transformation took place in the seminaries, it would be more beneficial for society. But I returned unsuccessful. In the year 1372, after much pressure, I came and bought a house in Tehran and returned to Tehran to live. Again some of the gentlemen insisted that no, stay in the seminary. I gave back the very house I had bought in Tehran, and returned to Qom once more, staying there another seven years until the year 1379. But I saw that everything was falling apart.

Central Bank's final blow to the phantom deposits of trust companies

What is phantom depositing?

🔹Phantom depositing by trust companies referred to a phenomenon where the deposit of export earnings was reported to the bank, but upon attempting to use the funds, it turned out that no financial transfer had actually taken place.

🔹Last winter, the scale of phantom depositing by trust companies reached such levels that the government faced a dollar shortage. This shortage is considered one of the factors behind the government's decision to eliminate the preferential exchange rate.

What is the Central Bank's new mechanism?

🔹Under the Central Bank's new framework, trust companies must first transfer a specified amount, and only after full verification by the Central Bank do they receive authorization to move larger sums.

entry.title: [bamotamem] Some people only see and touch the ground they were standing on after they…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @bamotamem

Some people only see and touch the ground they were standing on after they fall.

First explanation

In the early years of Motamem, when we started the daily sentences, sometimes I would also put some of my own words among the daily sentences at the top of the site.

After a while, I felt it wasn't a nice thing to do. The people whose words we were quoting were great people; thinkers, opinion-makers, and at the very least, well-known. Putting my own words among those people's words wasn't a nice thing to do.

I have no problem with saying and writing my words separately (I've been busy with exactly that my whole life). But that thing wasn't mature. In short, consider the photo-note above as the youthful transgressions caused by rawness.

Second explanation

Eleven years ago, when I gave a talk about personal branding, I ended my speech with a sentence that I still like and still stand by. Since the underlying theme of that sentence was also falling, it came to mind now:

Not everyone falls downward,
some fall upward.

#جمله‌های_روزانه_متمم

Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation confirmed on Saturday, 18 Mehr, that operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh have been suspended following an attack on the airport that wounded a number of people. A diplomatic source told Agence France-Presse that Yemen's Houthis attacked the airport with a missile at around three in the afternoon local time. According to initial reports, dozens of people were wounded in the attack. The Wall Street Journal also reported, citing Saudi officials, that missiles fired by the Houthis struck Terminal 3 of the airport directly. A hospital source told Agence France-Presse that five of the wounded are in intensive care. An eyewitness also said that while at Gate 403 of the domestic flights terminal, he saw a missile strike the area of Gate 401 and passengers being wounded. The witness told Agence France-Presse: "I saw Gate 401 being hit and people wounded before my eyes. Everyone was fleeing." Saturday's attack came after Riyadh airport had already been targeted by Houthi attacks on Wednesday and Thursday. Those attacks left a total of four dead and several wounded, and caused serious damage to a passenger plane belonging to a Saudi airline. Three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, were killed in Thursday's attacks, and one Sudanese citizen in Wednesday's attack. The Houthis have claimed responsibility for the attacks. The escalation of missile attacks on Saudi Arabia comes amid the resumption of widespread clashes between the Houthis and Riyadh-backed government forces in Yemen.@VahidHeadline 📡 @VahidOnline

The Human Rights Activists in Iran collective announced in a report marking the World Day Against the Death Penalty that over the past year, 2,003 people were executed in Iran, at least 69 of whom faced political and security charges. The number of executions during this period rose by about 29 percent compared to the same period previously, climbing from 1,553 to 2,003 — the highest figure recorded across 10 reporting periods. According to the report's statistics, executions increased from 505 in the 2016–2017 period to 2,003 in the 2025–2026 period. Broken down by type of charge, 57.56 percent were for murder and 36.25 percent for drug offenses. entry.title: [darvishnameh] Superadobe is an expanded method of the same old adobe, using long bags filled…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @darvishnameh

Superadobe is an expanded method of the same old adobe, using long bags filled with moistened soil and then tamped down for proper compaction. The bags are stacked row by row in a circular plan, rising uniformly to form a dome. To prevent the bags from shifting and also to resist earthquakes, barbed wire is used between the layers, acting like mortar to bind the rows together and helping give the structure an integrated, chain-like quality that gives it high resistance to earthquakes and other events. In this structure, due to the dome form, the thickness of the walls, and the natural materials used, heat exchange with the outside is minimized and energy loss is managed dramatically. Superadobe was invented by Nader Khalili, an Iranian architect, and is now recognized worldwide as one of the methods for building sustainable and natural homes. In the Name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful
📌The oppressed and cowardly martyrdom of the martyred Dr. Nusrat Eftekhari, Deputy for Cultural and Social Affairs of the Police Command of Sistan and Baluchestan Province, on the path of serving the people, is a bitter and sorrowful loss. 📌I, while offering my condolences and congratulations on the martyrdom of this striving woman to her esteemed family, comrades, colleagues, and the noble people of Sistan and Baluchestan and Islamic Iran, beseech from the presence of God Almighty elevated ranks for that exalted martyred woman and patience and tranquility for the bereaved.

Will Iran launch a preemptive strike before the American election? In Washington, this scenario is being taken seriously. The logic goes like this: Tehran's clock is an hourglass, and every day the sanctions erode the economy further. If Tehran is certain that after November 2 it will be attacked regardless, waiting means losing. So the best moment to strike is a few weeks before the election. Iran would both demonstrate its power and knock Trump down at the ballot box, because any response from America would drag the war into the middle of election season. But this calculation has one big hole: January 3, the day the new American Congress begins its work. From November 2 until that day, Trump is neither worried about votes nor dealing with a new Congress. On the other side, until the election, Trump sees any war as harmful to himself and buys time. Every day he buys time is an advantage for Tehran and reduces the incentive to preempt. So everything comes back to a question that James Fearon has called the "commitment problem": Does Tehran believe that after the election it will not be attacked? If it believes so, preemption makes no sense. If it does not, Schelling's dark room may at any moment ring out with the sound of gunfire.@sadegh_alhosseini

entry.title: [Soroushdabbagh_Official] Excerpts from my recent interview with the IBNA book news agency: "If Sohrab…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @Soroushdabbagh_Official

Excerpts from my recent interview with the IBNA book news agency: "If Sohrab were alive today, in the third millennium and in today's Tehran, and were present at his exhibitions, which part of what he had to say would be more worth hearing, and what would your first question to him be?" In my view, Sohrab's calmness, composure, and Stoic way of being would take on great significance; a subject about which much could be said separately. This calmness manifests in his lovemaking with and proximity to nature and a kind of "ataraxia," meaning inner tranquility, which the Stoic philosophers spoke about. Sohrab had internalized this calmness and also looked upon the world with a poetic gaze. The critique of technology, which I spoke about earlier, death-awareness and the effort to give meaning to life are also among the hearable and contemporary parts of his thought. Loving nature, paying attention to the other, and reflecting on categories such as death, love, solitude, and suffering can, in my view, still be worth hearing today. Regarding the exhibition of his paintings that you mentioned, naturally the paintings themselves matter; but I think Sohrab's words about the world and his way of living are also very important today. The reason is that in his case, there was considerable overlap between his public and private life, between his lived life and his work. He lived the way he wrote, and especially the way he composed poetry. This overlap and what we call "authenticity" can make a person charismatic and influence others; an unpretentious and intimate influence, such that one could benefit from his company and not feel the passage of time. In such conditions, the person's own presence and way of living become as important as his words. If I want to answer your question, "If you saw Sohrab, what would your first question to him be?" The truth is, I might not have had any specific question at all. For more than thirty years I have been living in Sohrab's atmosphere. Perhaps I would have liked to watch him; or, to put it better, to spend time in his company from noon until night, to chat together and experience that composure and calmness that was in his being, in socializing with him. I wanted to benefit, to the extent of my capacity, from that calmness that I believe had descended upon him. Sohrab himself said: "We ourselves are the awning of our calmness." I would have liked to catch and experience a breeze of that composure and calmness from his company... When you know someone well and are familiar with their life-world, sometimes sitting in silence itself, and even conversation without sound, can be valuable and instructive.👇👇👇 https://www.instagram.com/reel/DeR92wHRn21/?dlrf=dXF3aTRnY2t1ZTVs

entry.title: [fazelimohammadir] A man of building ▪️ Mohsen Khalili Iraqi passed away today, 17 Mehr 1405.…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @fazelimohammadir

A man of building ▪️ Mohsen Khalili Iraqi passed away today, 17 Mehr 1405. A man whose name was intertwined with industry, entrepreneurship, and resilience. His passing marks the loss of one of the enduring figures of Iran's industry. An industrialist whose life demonstrated that building a factory is only the beginning of the journey, and that the greater art lies in keeping it alive through difficult times and passing it on to future generations. ▪️ Khalili Iraqi, born in 1308, grew up in a family where work and initiative held a special place. His father, Mahmoud Khalili, was one of the pioneers of Iran's industry, and Mohsen set out alongside him on a path that led to the founding of Butan. Father and son saw an opportunity to improve people's lives in the gases that flared above the oil wells. The fruit of this vision was the expansion of liquid gas use and subsequently the production of gas appliances, which wove industry into the daily lives of Iranian families. ▪️ He belonged to a generation that saw industry as a path to the nation's prosperity. Involvement in industrial associations and efforts to strengthen cooperation among producers formed another part of his legacy. In this vision, the progress of one factory was inseparable from the fate of other enterprises, and defending production required cooperation and organization among industrialists. His professional life, of course, was not without hardship. After the revolution, part of Butan's shares were subject to confiscation orders, and the Khalili family struggled for years to reclaim them. From what I have heard, Mohsen Khalili appeared in court 254 times to win back his company. He and his partners, in order to keep the company afloat and pay the workers' wages, even sold their personal properties. This act of standing firm is one of the brightest chapters of his life. ▪️ In his final years, the concern for development never left his mind. He dedicated part of his wealth to industrial research, and through the establishment of the Mohsen Khalili Iraqi Industrial Development Foundation, he supported the study of the challenges of Iran's industrialization. Supporting economists' research was a continuation of the very path he had begun decades earlier in the workshop and the factory. An effort to find ways to build a more prosperous Iran. From the bottom of my heart, I offer my condolences to the honorable family and friends of Engineer Khalili on his passing. May his soul rest in peace and his memory be cherished ☑️ Mohsen Jalalpour mohsenjalalpour

The historical instance of this view can also be found in history. In Book Five of the History of the Peloponnesian War, written by Thucydides, the dialogue between the Melians and the Athenians is detailed.

The story was that in 416 BC, Athens asked the small island of Melos to surrender to its empire. The Melians tried to maintain their neutrality and hoped that justice, independence, and the possibility of help from Sparta would protect them, but the Athenians stated their argument clearly:

"The issue is not only our present enemies; independent islands like you are also a danger to the empire, because they stand outside our order... if peoples maintain their independence, it is because they have power; and if we do not attack them, it is because we fear them. So by subjugating you, in addition to expanding our empire, we also increase our security; especially since you are islanders and weaker than others and should not be able to prevail over the masters of the sea."

With Love and Without Love

"Duty without love becomes tedious; duty performed with love makes one steadfast. Responsibility without love makes one inconsiderate; responsibility borne with love makes one caring. Justice without love makes one hard-hearted; justice practiced with love makes one trustworthy. Upbringing without love becomes contentious; upbringing carried out with love makes one patient. Wisdom without love makes one cunning; wisdom exercised with love makes one understanding. Kindness without love becomes hypocritical; kindness shown with love makes one benevolent. Order without love leads to fault-finding; order upheld with love makes one open-minded. Knowledge and expertise without love make one self-righteous; knowledge and expertise applied with love make one trustworthy. Power without love makes one violent; power wielded with love makes one helpful. Dignity without love makes one arrogant; dignity upheld with love makes one humble. Wealth without love makes one miserly; wealth used with love makes one generous. Faith without love makes one fanatical; faith lived with love makes one peaceable."

Source: unknown author; as cited in Hans Küng, Was ich glaube, München: Piper Verlag, 2009, pp. 268–269. Translated from the German text. [Sourcing and translation by artificial intelligence]

1 – 7 January 2023: Can the power of love truly change life? Some simple antitheses by an author unknown to me make clear how greatly love, as a fundamental attitude, is able to transform life:

"Duty without love makes one peevish; duty fulfilled in love makes one constant. Responsibility without love makes one ruthless; responsibility borne in love makes one caring. Justice without love makes one hard; justice practiced in love makes one reliable. Upbringing without love makes one contradictory; upbringing undertaken in love makes one patient. Cleverness without love makes one cunning; cleverness practiced in love makes one understanding. Friendliness without love makes one hypocritical; friendliness shown in love makes one kind. Order without love makes one petty; order maintained in love makes one generous. Expertise without love makes one opinionated; expertise exercised in love makes one trustworthy. Power without love makes one violent; power employed in love makes one helpful. Honor without love makes one haughty; honor preserved in love makes one modest. Possession without love makes one miserly; possession used in love makes one generous. Faith without love makes one fanatical; faith lived in love makes one peaceable."

Source: @VahidOnline

Margaret Hamilton, an American scientist and one of the pioneers of software engineering who played a key role in landing the first American astronauts on the Moon, has died at the age of 90. She led a team of experts who designed and developed the software used in NASA's Apollo space missions. MIT, confirming Hamilton's death, announced that she passed away on Wednesday, the eighth of Mehr 1405, corresponding to September 30, 2026. In a statement, the institute described Hamilton as one of the pioneers of computer science who played an important role in developing the field before software engineering became a widespread profession. Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and headed the software engineering division. The group she managed designed the guidance and control software for the Apollo 11 spacecraft, which played a decisive role in the historic landing of Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the Moon in 1969. During this mission, the spacecraft's computer encountered a processing overload moments before landing, but the software designed by Hamilton's group was able to continue the landing operation by prioritizing tasks. Barack Obama, the former president of the United States, awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016 in recognition of Hamilton's scientific achievements and her role in advancing space technology. @VahidOOnLine📡 @VahidOnline

entry.title: [VahidOnline] Reuters reported on Thursday, 16 Mehr, that the number of ships transiting the…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @VahidOnline

Reuters reported on Thursday, 16 Mehr, that the number of ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz has fallen to its lowest level in more than two months, following a surge in attacks on oil tankers last week. Citing data and analysis from the analytics firm Kpler, Reuters reported that only 7 commercial vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday — the lowest figure since the first of Mordad. Crude oil transit through the strait also dropped 27 percent from the wartime peak the previous week, falling to at least 10.1 million barrels per day, equivalent to 74 percent of the pre-war level. According to Kpler analysts, most of this decline is attributable to ship-to-ship transfers of cargoes in the Sea of Oman. According to Reuters, however, exports from the coasts of the Sea of Oman and the Red Sea rose to 6.7 million barrels per day — more than double the pre-war level — helping to offset the reduced supply through the Strait of Hormuz. Kpler data shows the number of transiting ships rose to 10 on Wednesday, but remained far below the more than 20 vessels seen on Sunday and Monday. The report comes after attacks on oil tankers passing through the Strait of Hormuz last week reached their highest weekly level since the start of the Iran war. Before the war began on the ninth of Esfand last year, roughly 125 large commercial ships — including oil tankers, gas carriers, bulk carriers, and container ships — passed through the Strait of Hormuz daily. Meanwhile, Donald Trump, the President of the United States, posted a chart on Thursday on the Truth Social network showing that oil traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has returned to levels seen before the US and Israeli war against Iran.@VahidOOnLine📡 @VahidOnline

Reuters published an investigative report on Thursday, 16 Mehr, based on interviews with more than 75 human rights experts, lawyers, and Iranian citizens, writing that in the wake of the Dey protests, Iran is experiencing the most severe crackdown by the Islamic Republic in decades. According to Reuters, the Islamic Republic's security and judicial apparatuses, working in coordination with state-run broadcasting, are seeking to instill fear and silence dissent through rushed executions, closed-door trials, widespread judicial prosecutions, and the airing of forced confessions. According to the report, since 28 Esfand 1404, at least 34 people arrested in connection with the Dey protests have been executed. Five of them were executed in just the past 10 days. By contrast, over the four years following the 1401 protests, a total of 15 people were executed in connection with those protests. Reuters also reported that Armenian security officials warned a group of Iranian protesters in May about serious threats to their lives and urged them to leave the country to ensure their own safety and that of their families. Ashkan, a 30-year-old Iranian protester who attended the meeting with Armenian security officials, said they were warned that individuals had possibly been dispatched to abduct, assassinate, or harm them. Reuters said it corroborated his account with statements from another protester present at the same meeting and with an audio recording of that meeting. Reuters also reported that the Islamic Republic's security institutions have extended pressure on critics beyond Iran's borders by threatening the families of opposition figures living abroad who are inside Iran, revoking passports, and refusing to provide consular services. @VahidOOnLine📡 @VahidOnline

entry.title: [jalaeipour] "He was so humble and self-effacing that he had no idea of his own greatness."…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @jalaeipour

"He was so humble and self-effacing that he had no idea of his own greatness."

In his autobiography, the late Arthur Arberry writes of the late Reynold A. Nicholson — scholar, commentator, and translator of literary and mystical works from Persian and Arabic into English:

He was a consummate scholar, so enamored of his books that he sacrificed his eyesight to ceaseless reading, so humble and self-effacing that he had no idea of his own greatness. In the final years of his life, when the lamp of his eyes was flickering toward extinction, he composed this verse — a poem that, to me, among all the last words ever uttered by human beings, carries the truest inspiration and the most moving farewell:

When Truth appears unveiled before your eyes,
These tongues are left bewildered and surprised.
*I shall fall silent — the Beloved has come to speak:*
*Listen, and God knows best what is right and true.*
*Become devoid of sense, of hearing, and of thought,*
*That you may hear the summons "Return!"*
As long as this tongue remains, you shall not hear the Word.
So words must be brief. And peace.

**I have borrowed the Persian rendering of Nicholson's poem from verses of the Masnavi. The asterisked lines are from the Masnavi.

- Nicholson's poem, as narrated by Arberry, reads:
When Truth shines out words fail and nothing tell;
Now hear the Voice within your hearts. Farewell.

This is the closing verse of a long poem that Arberry quoted and confirmed earlier in this same piece, noting that in these verses Nicholson was deeply influenced by Rumi: ... He seldom spoke of his personal beliefs, and I, too, in twenty-five years of close friendship with him, learned little about how he was raised or of his spiritual journey. Yet the image that took shape in my mind was that he, like many others, had lost his faith in youth and then recovered it through intellectual companionship and kinship of spirit with Muslim mystics.

In his old age, he composed a poem in which, for the first time, he laid bare his innermost thoughts. It was clear that these thoughts had been profoundly shaped by long years of studying Rumi's works ...

Mohammad Mehdi Mojahedi

🔸With the onset of the cold season, the gas imbalance will become apparent, especially in the north of the country; therefore, the president, who is heading to Turkmenistan today, must pursue the import and swap of gas from the northern neighbor.

🔸According to our reporter, our country, due to its vast geography and the unparalleled coverage of the household gas network, along with the dependence of power plants and various industries on gas fuel, has faced an imbalance between production and consumption. The enemy's attack on South Pars during the 40-day war, although it met with Iran's decisive and unexpected response to the gas facilities of "Ras Laffan" and caught the enemy off guard, part of the country's gas production was also damaged and the imbalances worsened.

🔸Damage to five phases of the South Pars refineries during the Ramadan war reduced the country's daily gas production capacity by about 230 million cubic meters. So far, according to the National Gas Company, 95 million cubic meters of gas have returned to the grid, and currently there is a deficit of 135 million cubic meters of gas.

🔸If the upcoming winter is similar to last year's winter in terms of temperature and consumption, and only 95 million cubic meters of the damaged capacity is restored, the gas deficit will be about 130 million cubic meters, which, combined with the previous imbalance figure, will total about 380 million cubic meters per day.

🔸The gas shortage problem is not limited to homes, and power plants, in order to prevent power outages for household subscribers, are forced to turn to alternative fuels, namely diesel and fuel oil. The increased consumption of fuel oil, or mazut, also leads to an increase in pollutants and worsening air pollution.

🔸Of course, gas imports from Turkmenistan also face obstacles. The story of gas imports from this country began with a 25-year contract concluded between the parties in 1997, but due to financial problems that arose during Bijan Zangeneh's ministry in Hassan Rouhani's government, it ran into trouble in subsequent years. Of course, the other side also had breaches of commitment, which ultimately, with the weak defense of the Iranian side in the legal dispute, resulted in our country being fined. This fine and its consequences have cast a shadow over oil transfers between the two countries in recent years.

🔸Despite all these problems, during the era of the martyred Raisi in the Thirteenth Government and with Iran's personal follow-up, Iran was able to receive the right of oil swap between Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan in the form of gas. "Our covenant with the sweet-lipped ones was sealed by God." As the birthday anniversary of Sohrab Sepehri—the celebrated contemporary poet and painter—approaches, and given my extensive Sepehri scholarship over the past two decades, two of my interviews about this modern Eastern seeker were published today in the newspaper "Iran" and the Iranian Book News Agency (IBNA). Dear enthusiasts and readers can access the interviews through my Telegram channel and website, or via the links below. Furthermore, thanks to my esteemed friend and researcher Mehrdad Mehrjoo, the PDF of the engaging book "Eyes of a Passage: A Narrative of Soroush Dabbagh's Sepehri Studies" has been published to coincide with Sepehri's birthday in mid-Mehr. The book features the author's thorough, empathetic, and critical re-reading of my writings on Sepehri's life-world, along with a curated selection of passages from my Sepehri research. The book file is available to those interested through both his and my Telegram channels: "Each of us had a sky in every bend of thought / every motion of our hand sang to the dawn with the beat of a wing. / Our pockets echoed with the chirping of childhood mornings. / We were a band of lovers, and our road / passed by familiar villages of poverty / toward boundless serenity. / Above a pool, heads bowed of their own accord: / night was evaporating from our faces / and the friend's voice reached the friend's ear." http://ibna.ir/x6KxY https://share.google/6VVbXc29XIPqOWyFY https://www.instagram.com/p/DeMf_QexiQr/?stkn=MWxpYXowOXQ2YjYx

The memory of the dollar's collapse in Mehr; 📢 Will history repeat itself and the dollar drop below 200,000 tomans? ◀️ The dollar has once again reached one of its historic peaks, and at the same time, the Central Bank has begun efforts to contain currency turmoil by increasing supply and intervening in the market. But the experience of the years 1397 and 1399 carries an important warning for today's buyers; in both periods, the dollar faced heavy declines after hitting a peak in Mehr. Now the question is: if past patterns repeat, how far can a 270,000-toman dollar retreat? 1️⃣ A decline similar to that of 1399 — about 33 percent — would bring the dollar to around 180,000 tomans. 2️⃣ Even a 28 percent correction similar to 1398 would put the price at about 194,000 tomans. 3️⃣ In a far more severe scenario, similar to the 1397 crash, a 46 percent drop could push the rate down to around 146,000 tomans. entry.title: [mostafamalekian] 🔴How can we make the most of middle age? We shouldn't expect our past selves…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @mostafamalekian

🔴How can we make the most of middle age? We shouldn't expect our past selves to have our present understanding. ✍Mostafa Malekian

Sometimes we look at the past and say: If I had spent those years doing something else, I would have a better life today. Why did I play so much as a child? Why did I pursue things in my youth that no longer matter to me today?

But in this judgment, we forget one thing: every period of life has its own demands. We cannot have had a childhood without having the interests and desires of childhood. We cannot have gone through youth and yet expect to have had our present maturity from the very beginning.

Part of our sorrow about the past comes from this very expectation — as if we wanted to have been as mature throughout our entire lives as we are today. Whereas it is precisely by going through those periods that we have reached this point.

▪️ Let us not see past mistakes as pure loss

Even a choice that we consider a mistake today may have brought us joys and friendships.

For example, we say, why did I pursue football instead of studying? But how much happiness has that same football given us? What friendships did it create that have stayed with us later in life?

If we only look at the costs of a choice and dismiss all the good things that came from it, we will not have a complete picture of the past.

▪️ No life is all benefit and no cost

Every way of life opens up possibilities before us and also carries costs. We cannot compare our lived life with an imaginary life that has all the good things and pays no price for them.

▪️ Let us seize the remaining opportunities

Not all opportunities are lost with the end of youth. There are still things we can begin, things we can learn, and pleasures we can experience.

If we spend today only on regret for yesterday, in a few more years, today will also become a new subject for regret.

Instead of only lamenting lost opportunities, let us treasure the opportunities not yet lost.

📚 Mostafa Malekian | Lecture on the book "Philosophical Guidance for Middle Age"
@mostafamalekian

🔸JD Vance, the Vice President of the United States, says the Iranian government must "meaningfully" reduce its uranium enrichment capacity to end the war, and that the United States will not settle for verbal promises in negotiations with the Islamic Republic — it demands concrete action from Tehran.

And if you want to demonstrate your commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don't produce highly enriched fuel. This is a very basic and decisive issue."
